item.title: Three Dating Profile Mistakes That Attract the Wrong People
item.description:
Mating

Three Dating Profile Mistakes That Attract the Wrong People

How to get the right kind of attention without losing yourself in the process

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • People want to stand out in a crowded dating field.
  • They often confuse getting attention with attracting what they actually want.
  • What you present matters, but how you present it may matter just as much.
Source: Tom Fisk / Pexels

While watching my students struggle to find compatible partners on dating apps, I began noticing the same mistakes again and again. Some profiles revealed almost nothing; others revealed too much. Some leaned heavily on sexualized images, while many simply disappeared into a sea of interchangeable profiles.

I started wondering: What actually makes a dating profile stand out in a way that creates genuine interest—and perhaps leads to a compatible match—rather than simply attracting attention?

That question led my colleagues and me to study three aspects of dating profiles: the photos people choose, how much they disclose, and how they present that information. Across these studies, a common theme emerged: How you present yourself shapes not only how potential partners see you, but also what they think you want—and whether they can imagine connecting with you.

Mistake 1: Trying too hard to look sexy

In online dating, the first filter is often visual. People tend to notice photos before reading anything else, and on apps that create a sense of endless alternatives, a profile that fails to pass that initial threshold may never get a second look.

So it makes sense that people want to choose their sexiest photos. But that strategy can backfire.

In our research (read more here), sexualized profiles led viewers to perceive their owners as more interested in casual sex and as less suitable long-term partners. Sexualization may draw attention to the body while pushing other qualities—intelligence, warmth, responsiveness, or simply the sense that there is an interesting person behind the picture—into the background.

You can win attention in a second and still lose the chance to be seen for who you are.

The solution isn’t to make yourself less attractive. It’s to let more of yourself come through. Choose flattering but authentic photos that show different facets of your life rather than a collection of disconnected glamour shots.

Mistake 2: Saying either too little or too much

The amount you disclose matters too.

Our research (read more here) suggests a Goldilocks pattern: Moderate self-disclosure tends to be more effective than revealing either very little or a great deal.

A nearly empty profile can send a message you may not intend. Viewers may interpret sparse information as low effort, lack of interest in closeness, or even an attempt to hide something. Importantly, the amount people disclosed also shaped perceptions of their relationship goals: Greater disclosure tended to signal greater interest in a long-term relationship.

But more is not always better. Very high disclosure was less effective than moderate disclosure in attracting potential partners. Too much information may become overwhelming, feel premature, or expose every possible incompatibility before there is enough connection to put those differences in context.

There is no magical word count. Reveal enough to give someone a meaningful sense of who you are and to signal that you are genuinely invested in connecting—but leave something to discover on the first date.

Mistake 3: Listing qualities instead of bringing yourself to life

Even the right amount of information can disappear into the crowd if everyone is saying essentially the same thing.

“I’m easygoing, ambitious, and always up for an adventure.”

Lovely. So are half the people on the app.

Our research (read more here) suggests that how you present yourself may be as important as what you reveal. When the same basic information was structured as a story rather than a list of traits, it elicited greater empathy. That empathy, in turn, predicted greater romantic interest.

A story doesn’t have to be long. Dating apps are hardly the place for your memoir. A tiny anecdote can do the work.

Instead of “I love cooking,” imagine:
“I cook like I’m on a competitive reality show, except there are no cameras, no prize money, and I still haven’t found a judge brave enough to taste the results.”

Instead of “I love traveling,” try:
“I’m excellent at planning trips right up until I arrive, at which point I ignore the itinerary and follow whichever street smells best.”

The point isn’t to manufacture clever lines. It’s to provide a small window into how you think, what makes you laugh, and what distinguishes you from the dozens of other attractive strangers competing for the same person’s attention.

Stories help turn a profile owner from a bundle of desirable traits into a person someone can begin to imagine knowing.

Don’t sell yourself. Make yourself recognizable.

Dating profiles inevitably involve self-promotion, and some principles borrowed from marketing can help people stand out. But you are not a product, and the goal shouldn’t be to construct the most marketable version of yourself.

The real challenge is getting the right kind of attention without losing yourself in the process.

We all want to be chosen and loved for who we genuinely are, not simply for the shiny armor we put on to attract someone. A profile that generates enormous interest but creates the wrong impression has not really succeeded.

The best profile doesn’t try to make you irresistible to everyone. It gives compatible people enough information to become curious about this particular person—and a reason to think, Why this one? What is it about us that might make us click?

And if that curiosity leads to a date, the person who shows up should be recognizably the same person they wanted to meet.

item.title: Why Are Psychiatric Medications Still Stigmatized?
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

Why Are Psychiatric Medications Still Stigmatized?

How social beliefs about psychiatric drugs can influence treatment decisions.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Negative beliefs about medication can become internalized and affect self-esteem.
  • Stigma may contribute to a person avoiding or discontinuing psychiatric treatment.
  • Reducing stigma means challenging stereotypes without ignoring treatment risks.
Source: Gabrielle Wright / Unsplash

Psychiatric medications are widely used in the treatment of mental health conditions. They include antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, and other medications used to treat psychiatric symptoms and disorders.

Yet taking a psychiatric medication is not always a simple medical decision. People may worry about side effects, question whether they really need it, or struggle with the idea of taking a drug for a mental health condition in the first place.

These concerns can have different causes, but some of them are not related to the medication itself. They come from what psychiatric medication represents in our society. For example, a pill can be seen as evidence that someone is “really sick,” as a sign of weakness or dependence, or as something that separates a person from what is considered normal.

This is stigma, and it can have a real impact on how people perceive psychiatric treatment, whether they start it, and whether they continue taking it.

Understanding stigma

The word stigma means a mark, scar, or sign with a negative meaning. In society, it refers to prejudice or disapproval that devalues a person or a group.

When it comes to mental health, stigma can be directed at the psychiatric condition itself or at its treatment. Although the two are closely related, they should not be treated as the same thing.

A person may, for example, understand that depression is a medical condition while believing that antidepressants are unnecessary, dangerous, or a sign that someone is unable to deal with life without medication. The opposite can also happen. Someone may have no particular prejudice against psychiatric medications while feeling ashamed of having a psychiatric diagnosis.

There is also a difference between what society thinks about psychiatric medications and what the person taking them comes to believe about themselves. External stigma can become internalized, turning social stereotypes into personal beliefs. A person may begin to see themselves as weak, dependent, incapable, or fundamentally different from other people simply because they need medication.

This is particularly relevant when we look at treatment decisions. Refusing or discontinuing a medication may sometimes be an attempt to avoid not only its adverse effects, but also the meaning attached to taking it.

How does stigma manifest?

Because stigma involves negative stereotypes and prejudice that permeate society, its manifestations can vary depending on the culture and social environment in which a person lives.

In general, however, some patterns tend to be relatively consistent:

  • Self-stigma, when a person internalizes negative stereotypes and prejudices about mental illness or its treatment.
  • Lower self-esteem, as internalized stigma can affect how a person sees themselves and their own abilities.
  • Avoidance of the psychiatric label, which may lead a person to reject or avoid treatment in an attempt to distance themselves from the identity associated with mental illness.

Stigma may also influence how a person anticipates the effects of a medication. This is relevant to the nocebo effect, in which negative expectations about a treatment can contribute to the perception or worsening of adverse effects.

The relationship between stigma, expectations, and the nocebo effect is complex and deserves a separate discussion.

This matters because concerns about psychiatric medications can affect treatment decisions even before a person takes the first dose. And when long-term adherence is already challenging, anything that makes someone less willing to start or continue treatment deserves attention.

How can we reduce the stigma surrounding psychiatric medications?

There is no simple way to eliminate social stigma, since it is influenced by cultural beliefs and the way mental illness is understood in society. But some changes can help reduce it:

  • Better information: Understanding what psychiatric medications are, what they do, and what their limitations are can help replace misconceptions with more realistic expectations.
  • Separating treatment from identity: Taking a psychiatric medication does not mean that a person is weak, incapable, or fundamentally different from other people.
  • Normalizing psychiatric treatment: Psychiatric medications are medications used to treat medical conditions. Their use should not be treated as something shameful or something that needs to be hidden.
  • Questioning stereotypes: Ideas such as “psychiatric medication changes who you are,” “people who take it are weak,” or “once you start, you will never be able to stop” can influence how people perceive treatment, even when they are not accurate.

The goal is not to create a positive image of psychiatric medications at all costs. It is to make sure that social stigma does not become part of the decision about whether a treatment is right for someone.
